content: The insertion of a grommet, also known as a ventilation tube or tympanostomy tube, into the tympanic membrane is a frequently performed surgical procedure in high-income countries. This operation is primarily indicated for two conditions: chronic otitis media with effusion (chronic OME, also referred to as glue ear) associated with conductive hearing loss, and recurrent acute otitis media (AOM). Other less common indications include acute mastoiditis and middle ear atelectasis. The primary goal of grommet insertion in cases of chronic OME is to improve hearing by equalizing the pressure between the middle ear and the external ear canal. This process facilitates the release of negative pressure in the middle ear and promotes the natural drainage of fluid through the Eustachian tube. In cases of recurrent AOM, the aim is to reduce the frequency and severity of infections by allowing middle ear effusions to drain through the grommet into the external ear canal. However, these benefits are compromised if the grommet becomes obstructed. Grommet obstruction is a common complication that typically occurs before the grommet is naturally extruded, which usually happens around six to eight months after insertion. Early obstruction, defined as occurring within four weeks of surgery, can prevent the intended benefits of the procedure and is a source of frustration for patients, their families, and clinicians. Early obstruction is often caused by middle ear effusions present at the time of surgery or by blood solidifying within the grommet lumen. Later obstruction may result from otorrhoea, wax accumulation, or granulation tissue formation. A meta-analysis of ventilation tube complications estimated that the cumulative incidence of grommet obstruction at any point during follow-up was 6.9%, with a range of 0% to 37.3% depending on the population studied. In a study of 248 children undergoing grommet insertion for chronic OME in the United States, 10.6% of children had at least one blocked grommet at their first follow-up visit, which occurred on average 25.9 days postoperatively. Risk factors for postoperative grommet obstruction in children with chronic OME include the presence of serous effusion at the time of surgery and a longer interval to the first postoperative follow-up. Factors such as sex, body mass index, and the type of procedure (grommets alone versus grommets with adenoidectomy or adenotonsillectomy) did not appear to influence obstruction rates. Clinically, grommet obstruction is diagnosed using otoscopy, with or without tympanometry. Tympanometry provides an objective method for assessing grommet patency. However, the incidence of obstruction may be underestimated if routine follow-up is delayed for several months, as is common in many clinical settings. Early signs of obstruction may include the recurrence of symptoms or a lack of improvement as reported by patients or their caregivers. To prevent postoperative grommet obstruction, various strategies are employed. These include selecting grommets with specific physical properties, employing surgical techniques to minimize obstruction risk, and using pharmacological interventions during or after surgery. Grommets are available in different diameters, lengths, and materials, such as fluoroplastic, silicone, titanium, and stainless steel. Some grommets are coated with compounds like antibiotics, gold, human albumin, phosphorylcholine, or polyvinylpyrrolidone to reduce the risk of obstruction. For example, phosphorylcholine coatings may prevent biofilm formation on the grommet lumen, which could otherwise impede the clearance of middle ear effusions. Surgical techniques to prevent obstruction include suctioning middle ear effusions after myringotomy, which may improve hearing and reduce the risk of obstruction, although high-quality evidence supporting this practice is limited. Adrenaline-soaked gauze or saline instillation into the external ear canal may be used to achieve hemostasis and prevent blood clots from obstructing the grommet. Topical decongestants, such as oxymetazoline or phenylephrine, may also reduce the risk of obstruction by promoting vasoconstriction and improving hemostasis. Additionally, topical hydrogen peroxide may prevent obstruction by facilitating platelet aggregation and thrombus formation. Pharmacological interventions, including antibiotics and steroids, may also play a role in preventing grommet obstruction. Antibiotics, whether topical or systemic, can address active infections associated with chronic OME or recurrent AOM. Middle ear fluid cultures in these conditions often identify pathogens such as Haemophilus influenzae and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Steroids may reduce the risk of obstruction by decreasing inflammatory mediators, reducing the viscosity of middle ear effusions, and modulating lymphoid tissue and surfactant production in the Eustachian tube. Despite the widespread use of these interventions, the evidence supporting their effectiveness in preventing postoperative grommet obstruction has not been systematically reviewed. Some interventions, such as aminoglycosides and hydrogen peroxide, carry risks of ototoxicity, while others may cause systemic side effects. The use of antibiotics also raises concerns about bacterial resistance. Furthermore, the additional costs associated with these interventions must be justified by evidence of clinical benefit. A systematic review of the literature is needed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of interventions for preventing postoperative grommet obstruction. This review should include a comprehensive assessment of the quality of evidence and consider a wide range of interventions. While previous Cochrane reviews have addressed related topics, such as the prevention and treatment of otorrhoea following grommet insertion, they have not explicitly focused on grommet obstruction as a primary outcome.
